 The U.S. Department of Agriculture is facing its second class-action lawsuit over Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) junk food purchasing rules after a court struck down restrictions in five states earlier this year. The lawsuit, filed November 18 by a cohort of SNAP recipients, asks the court to stop the USDA from approving food restriction waivers in 18 states and to bar it from approving new ones. In June, a federal judge vacated waivers in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia after finding the USDA had exceeded the authority relied on to approve the restrictions. SNAP junk food waivers have been implemented in almost half of U.S. states, though rules vary. Some states have blocked some or all of the purchases of unhealthy items like sugary snacks, desserts, soda and energy drinks using benefits. The changes, enacted by individual states but approved by the USDA, are part of a Trump administration effort to promote healthier diets in the federal food assistance program. SNAP, which serves more than 36 million people nationwide, is the largest nutrition program in the country. Recipients have benefits loaded onto electronic benefit transfer cards that they can use to purchase food at participating retailers. “Today we are asking the Court to extend the protection SNAP participants already won to every family in the remaining states with food purchase restrictions,” Jeffrey Shinder, founding partner at Shinder Cantor Lerner and a representative of the SNAP recipients, said in a statement emailed to Newsweek. Newsweek has contacted the USDA for comment via email. The Lawsuit The new lawsuit seeks to extend the June legal victory of five SNAP recipients, using the same basis that the USDA exceeded its legal authority in granting the waivers and failed to follow its own advance notice requirements. As it stands, there are active or pending SNAP junk food waivers in Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia and Wyoming, according to the USDA's tracker. The lawsuit asks the court to vacate the waiver approvals and stop the agency from approving future waivers under the same authority. "USDA approved every waiver on materially identical terms and implemented a single federal framework to enforce the waivers against every SNAP retailer in the waiver States," the complaint reads. "The result is a set of unlawful waivers, all stemming from the same unlawful course of conduct driven by USDA." Plaintiffs in the case also argue the restrictions are unfair and do not take into account the different needs of SNAP recipients. Tamara Wagner, a diabetic plaintiff in North Dakota, said she relies on candy to manage drops in blood sugar and needs diet soda to help manage nausea for another health condition. Due to the restrictions, she says she has been rationing drinks and experiencing unstable blood sugar levels. The plaintiffs are 17 SNAP recipients and the South Carolina Convenience & Petroleum Marketers Association. The Trump Administration View Supporters argue the waivers let states steer taxpayer-funded SNAP benefits toward healthier food and help tackle obesity, diabetes and other diet-related diseases. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, who is named in the filing, said earlier this year the restrictions bring "SNAP back to its core principle of nutrition" and that she hopes "to sign waivers for all 50 states soon, and promote healthy foods for all Americans." Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has similarly backed the push. "We cannot continue a system that forces taxpayers to fund programs that make people sick and then pay a second time to treat the illnesses those very programs help create," he said in late 2025.
